title: Xuyun’s Chan Method
author: Compiled and narrated by Zhanran
excerpt: The essence of Chan investigation: probe toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted.

inline.s: The essence of Chan investigation: investigate toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted.
The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises.
This moment before a single thought arises is called non-arising;
not restless, not drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness—this is called non-ceasing.
At all times, solely this single thought,
turning the light back to reflect upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing” is called looking into the huatou, or attending to the huatou.
To investigate, thought after thought without interval, toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted, is called the doubt.
The Instructions of the Venerable Grand Master

Editor’s note: Master Xuyun was a giant of the Chan school, one who had passed through and awakened utterly to the truth. His instructions on the Chan Dharma are subtle and to the point, wholly unlike the notions of those who take things for granted (who cobble together a few words to say), unlike idle tangles of vines and wild-fox Chan—there is no falsehood in his words. In these instructions the Master lays out the whole of the true work of investigating Chan and awakening; yet because his words are terse and their meaning full, and his starting point is rather high, one needs a certain foundation to savor their true meaning and apply it in one’s own study and practice. If you are a newcomer to the Chan gate, it is best to practice first according to
Investigative Buddha-Recitation
. Once you have a certain foundation, then read Xuyun’s Chan Method closely and repeatedly, and you will surely receive great benefit.

blocks.text: Prologue

inline.s: Question: What is the huatou? What is looking into the huatou? What is the doubt?
Answer: Elder Master Xuyun said:
“What is meant by huatou? Hua is speech, and tou is what precedes speech. For instance, reciting ‘Amitābha Buddha’ is a word; before the recitation,
that is
the huatou
The so-called huatou

, is the very moment before a single thought arises; the moment a thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word. This moment before a thought arises is called non-arising; not restless, not drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness, is called non-ceasing.
At all times, solely this single thought, turning the light back to reflect upon this ‘non-arising and non-ceasing,’
is called
looking into the huatou

, or attending to the huatou.” “You must know that the true huatou is to be investigated toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted; without distinguishing activity from stillness, thought after thought without interval,
this is called
the doubt
(Without distinguishing activity from stillness, to investigate, thought after thought without interval, toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted, is called the doubt.)

[Non-arising and non-ceasing] The “non-arising and non-ceasing” spoken of here means: a single thought does not arise, and the investigation does not cease (not restless, not drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness). [Restlessness (diāojǔ)] The agitation of the mind. [Without distinguishing activity from stillness, thought after thought without interval] Whether in activity or in stillness, to investigate, thought after thought without interval, toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted. On this, Elder Master Xuyun instructs below:

“As for what is called activity and stillness, the beginner in study cannot but investigate it. Walking, standing, being in the hall, at work, receiving and seeing off guests, talking and laughing, urinating and defecating—these are called activity; sitting and lying down in quietness are called stillness. Thus
(in this way)
examine it subtly: in the course of the six periods of the day and night, at what time am I in activity without being carried off by activity
(still investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? At what time am I in stillness without being turned by stillness
(still investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? In the presence of all circumstances, does the mind arise or not arise? If one can examine as before, then in activity, not being carried off by activity, one can be alert and still
(alert and at the same time still)
; in stillness, not being turned by stillness, one is still and alert
(still and at the same time alert)

Question: The so-called huatou is simply a sentence. Why then did Elder Master Xuyun say that the huatou is what precedes speech? In the Chan Hall Instructions of the Convenient Teachings of Master Xuyun, he says:
“The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises; the moment a thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word.”

Answer: This was his kindly and skillful means. Some Chan practitioners have already reached “the ten thousand thoughts return to one” in their investigation, yet do not know to advance toward “the one returns to nothing,” and still cling to the huatou without letting go, thus stalling on the path of practice. So the Elder Master told them: the true huatou is what precedes speech; the very moment before a thought arises is the true huatou. In the Old Master Xuyun’s Letter on Chan, he says:

“You must know that the true huatou is to be investigated toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted; without distinguishing activity from stillness, thought after thought without interval, this is called the doubt.
(Without distinguishing activity from stillness, to investigate, thought after thought without interval, toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted, is called the doubt.)
Doubt on and doubt on, until it is beaten into a single mass. Turn the light back and shine upon it: who is it that doubts?

(Note: This is work in two steps: first, “investigate toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted ... until it is beaten into a single mass”; then, “turn the light back and shine upon it: who is it that doubts?”)
After a long, long time, when the melon ripens the stem falls, one suddenly touches the nostrils with which one was born
(thoroughly seeing one’s own nature)
, not obtained from outside.”
The method described above begins directly from no-thought,

investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted. For a Chan practitioner of beginner’s capacity, if “investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted” feels too hard to begin, he should first do the work of “the ten thousand thoughts return to one,”
following Elder Master Xuyun’s instructions on the transition from looking into the tail of the word to looking into the huatou.
In “Two Letters to Layman Jin Hongshu (1948),” Elder Master Xuyun says:

“If a beginner applies effort, he cannot but investigate from the tail of the word. For the sentient beings of the Latter Age of the Dharma are thick in obstructions and shallow in wisdom; without beginning from investigating the tail of the word, it is hard to reach the huatou; without applying effort where there is mind, it is hard to realize no-mind.”
In the Sobering Words on Chan Practice, Elder Master Xuyun says:
“If the huatou
(what precedes speech)

has not yet been taken up, and one’s delusive thoughts and drowsiness are many, you should still look into the word ‘who’ in ‘Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?’ When you have looked until delusive thoughts and drowsiness are few, and the word ‘who’ can no longer be forgotten, then look into the place where this thought arises. When a single thought does not arise, that is the unborn; to be able to see that a single thought is unborn is called truly looking into the huatou.”
Question: How does one practice “the ten thousand thoughts return to one”?
Answer: Elder Master Xuyun taught people to look into the word ‘who,’ and in this way to accomplish the ten thousand thoughts returning to one—returning upon the word ‘who.’ He said:

“If the huatou has not yet been taken up, and one’s delusive thoughts and drowsiness are many, you should still look into the word ‘who’ in ‘Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?’ When you have looked until delusive thoughts and drowsiness are few, and the word ‘who’ can no longer be forgotten, then look into the place where this thought arises.”

One may also practice in this way: raise a single phrase of the Buddha’s name, and at once turn inward with focused attention to peer (qù) into it: Who is reciting the Buddha’s name? After a while, raise the phrase of the Buddha’s name again, and at once turn inward with focused attention to peer into it: Who is reciting the Buddha’s name? Continue in this way. To peer inward with focused attention, free of delusive thoughts—this is the doubt. At first the doubt cannot stand its ground; while peering into “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” delusive thoughts spring up in thickets, because the peering is not focused and not continuous. After practicing for a time, the delusive thoughts gradually grow fewer; if a delusive thought arises, it means the peering lacks strength, and one must at once raise another phrase of the Buddha’s name, rouse one’s spirits, and peer inward with focused attention and continuity, and the delusive thought will vanish of itself. Later, the following state will appear: whenever one is peering into “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” there are no delusive thoughts; at this point the doubt has taken its stand. The next step is to let the doubt stand long and stand firm, until, the moment the Buddha’s name is raised, delusive thoughts vanish entirely and only the intention of peering inward into “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” remains. At this point the work of “the ten thousand thoughts return to one” is accomplished, and one should turn to the next stage, the study of “the one returns to nothing”: investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted.

If one cannot get a grip on the practice of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one in this way, or finds it very difficult, it shows that one’s power of awareness is too weak. One may first practice according to
Investigative Buddha-Recitation
, in the section “Preliminary Practices,” and once the foundation is laid, then practice the ten thousand thoughts returning to one.
Question: Please explain the path of Xuyun’s Chan method.

Answer: The path of Xuyun’s Chan method is: investigate the tail of the word → arouse the doubt (this is the doubt of investigating the tail of the word) → look into the huatou → arouse the doubt (this is the doubt of looking into the huatou, called the “true doubt”) → thoroughly see one’s own nature.

“The doubting thought of a beginner is very coarse, now broken off and now resumed, now familiar and now new. It does not count as the doubt; it may only be called thinking. Gradually, as the wild mind is reined in and the thought can be held a little steady, then it is called investigating. Further, as the effort gradually ripens, one doubts without intending to doubt; one no longer is aware of where one sits, nor does one know of body, mind, or world. Solely the thought of doubt appears before one, unbroken and uninterrupted, and only then is it called
the doubt

A Brief Biography of Master Xuyun:
A native of Xiangxiang in Hunan (

), of the lay surname Xiao. His given name was Guyan, his courtesy name Deqing. From the Republican era onward he was a great Chan worthy who transmitted the Dharma of the Caodong line while also inheriting the Linji line, revived the Yunmen line, upheld the Fayan line, and continued the Weiyang line—binding the dharma-lineages of the five houses in his single person. At nineteen he left home under the Venerable Changkai at Yongquan Monastery on Mount Gu in Fujian; the following year he received the complete precepts under the Venerable Miaolian. Thereafter he wandered on pilgrimage among the famous mountains, visiting teachers and seeking the Way, his footsteps reaching Sichuan, Xikang, Tibet, India, Ceylon, Burma, and other lands. At forty-three he made the vow to bow in pilgrimage to Mount Wutai, to repay the deep kindness of his parents. Setting out from Fahua Nunnery on Mount Putuo, he bowed once every three steps, and the journey took three years, enduring hunger and cold and three grave illnesses that brought him to the brink of death; each time he was saved by the response of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, until at last he bowed his way to Xiantong Monastery on Mount Wutai.

At fifty-six, at Gaomin Monastery in Jiangsu, when boiling water splashed his hand and the teacup fell to the ground, he suddenly cut through the root of doubt and awakened utterly to his original nature. At sixty-one he accompanied the two Dowager Courts on their westward journey at the end of the Qing, and there established a Dharma assembly for the protection of the nation and the averting of calamity. When it was over he withdrew into hiding on Mount Zhongnan, changed his name to Xuyun, and took the style Huanyou. Later he went to Penang, Malacca, Kuala Lumpur, Taiwan, and other places to expound scriptures and spread the Dharma. At sixty-eight, while expounding scriptures in Thailand, he once entered samādhi for nine days, astonishing the Thai capital. Afterwards, on behalf of Huguo Zhusheng Chan Monastery, he went to the capital to petition for the Buddhist canon. He persuaded Li Genyuan, the garrison commander of the Yunnan army, to quell (
mǐ

; to put down, to stop) the calamity of expelling monks and destroying monasteries. He also mediated the dispute between Han and Tibetan, pacified bandits, and removed the scourge of war for the people. He spread the teaching in Yunnan for eighteen years. At ninety he finally left Yunnan and returned to Mount Gu to serve as abbot.

At the age of one hundred and nine (1948) he spread the Dharma in Hong Kong. Then, bearing the compassionate vow to protect the teaching and save the monks, he returned to the mainland the following year.

, when the Master was one hundred and twelve, during the spring ordination the Yunmen Incident occurred; the Master was beaten again and again, his bones and sinews broken, until he fell unconscious. Before long illness struck, yet he sat cross-legged as before and took no food for nine days, whereupon came the matter of his spirit wandering to Tuṣita, attending upon Maitreya and hearing him expound the scriptures.
In his later years he dwelt at Mount Yunju in Jiangxi.
, in the autumn, he entered quiescence at Mount Yunju, aged one hundred and twenty by worldly reckoning, with one hundred and one years of monastic standing.

Taking his life as a whole, there was no practice he did not uphold: purity, asceticism, filial piety, patience, concentration, renunciation, compassion, the extraordinary, skillful means, fearlessness, and non-heedlessness. Lamenting that the spirit of the school had fallen into decay and the practice places lay in ruins (
yí

); that the Vinaya and the teachings were no longer heard, he made the vow to revive the ten-direction monasteries and rebuild the ancient temples. Among the famous practice places he restored are Huating Monastery in Yunnan (Yunqi), Jizu Zhusheng Chan Monastery, the Nanhua Monastery of Caoxi, Yongquan Monastery on Mount Gu in Fujian, Yunmen Chan Monastery at Qujiang in Guangdong, and Zhenru Chan Monastery on Mount Yunju in Jiangxi—more than eighty monasteries, nunneries, and halls great and small which he rebuilt. At the completion of each, he would find an abbot to take charge, and then quietly withdraw. Though the Master was a giant of the Chan school, he also constantly taught people to recite the Buddha’s name in all honesty. The books he wrote—The Profound Essentials of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, A Brief Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra, Annotations on the Sūtra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching, The Profound Meaning of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, and An Explanation of the Heart Sūtra—were all lost during the Yunmen Incident. Today only his Dharma words, instructions, letters, and poems survive, compiled by later hands into the single volume The Dharma Collection of Master Xuyun.

blocks.text: The Prerequisites for Investigating Chan

inline.s: (The original text is recorded from Master Xuyun’s Convenient Teachings.)
Put down all conditions; not a single thought arises.

The purpose of investigating Chan is to illuminate the mind and see the nature: that is, to do away with the pollution of one’s own mind and truly see the face of one’s own nature. Pollution means delusive thoughts and clinging; self-nature is the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtuous marks. The Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtuous marks are shared alike by all Buddhas and sentient beings, without the slightest difference. If one is free of delusive thoughts and clinging, one realizes one’s own Tathāgata wisdom and virtuous marks, and is a Buddha; otherwise one is a sentient being.
Only because
(only because)

you and I, from immeasurable kalpas past, have been lost and drowned in birth and death, and have been defiled so long that we cannot in an instant cast off delusive thoughts and truly see our own nature—and so we must investigate Chan. Hence the prerequisite for investigating Chan is to do away with delusive thoughts. How are delusive thoughts to be done away with? Śākyamuni Buddha said a great deal on this, but the simplest is the single word ‘rest’: ‘rest is bodhi.’ When the Chan school was brought to these eastern lands by Patriarch Bodhidharma, and after the Sixth Patriarch the Chan wind spread abroad and shook past and present, yet the most essential words spoken by Patriarch Bodhidharma and the Sixth Patriarch in instructing students were none other than ‘still all conditions, and not a single thought arises.’ To still all conditions is to put down all conditions,
and so these two phrases—‘put down all conditions, not a single thought arises’—are truly the prerequisite for investigating Chan
. If these two phrases are not put into practice, then as for investigating Chan, not only can one say there will be no success—even to enter the gate is impossible. For
(a conjunction, indicating cause)
with the ten thousand conditions entangling you and thought after thought arising and ceasing, can you even speak of investigating Chan?

[‘Put down all conditions, not a single thought arises’—these two phrases are truly the prerequisite for investigating Chan] In Xuyun’s Chan method, investigating Chan (looking into the huatou) means investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted. Therefore the non-arising of a single thought is the precondition for looking into the huatou (investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted); and to have not a single thought arise, one must put down all conditions.
‘Put down all conditions, not a single thought arises’ is the prerequisite for investigating Chan
(investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
. Since we now know this, how is it to be accomplished? For the highest, a single thought rests forever, straight through to the unborn, instantly realizing bodhi, with no entanglements at all
(no fuss)
. Next, one may
remove affairs by principle

. Know that self-nature is originally pure, that affliction and bodhi, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, are all merely names, and have nothing to do with my self-nature. Every thing and every matter is a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. This four-element body of mine, together with mountains, rivers, and the great earth, are within self-nature like foam upon the sea, rising and perishing as they will, without hindering the essence. One should not, following the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of illusory affairs, give rise to liking and loathing, taking up and casting off. Put the whole body down, like a dead man, and naturally the senses, their objects, and the consciousness-mind subside, and greed, hatred, delusion, and craving are extinguished. All the itch and pain, suffering and joy, hunger and cold, fullness and warmth, honor and disgrace, birth and death, disaster and blessing, ill and good fortune, praise and blame, gain and loss, safety and danger, peace and peril of this body—set them all outside one’s concern. Only this counts as putting down. Put down one, put down all, put down forever: this is called putting down all conditions. When all conditions are put down, delusive thoughts vanish of themselves, discrimination does not arise, and clinging is left far behind. At this point not a single thought arises, and the light of self-nature is revealed in its entirety. Now the conditions for investigating Chan are complete, and only then, applying effort in true investigation, does one have a share in illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.
[Foam (ōu)] Bubbles on the surface of water. Because they rise and vanish so easily, they are often used to liken the ever-changing affairs of the world and the brevity of life.

These days Chan practitioners often come to ask questions. Now the Dharma is fundamentally without dharma; once it falls into words, it is no longer the true meaning. Understand this one mind—it is originally Buddha; directly there is nothing to do, each is complete as he is; to speak of cultivation or of realization is all demon-talk. When Bodhidharma came east, he ‘pointed directly to the human mind; see the nature and become Buddha’—plainly and clearly he indicated that all sentient beings throughout the great earth are Buddhas: directly recognize this pure self-nature, accord with it without defilement, and through the six periods of the day and night, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, if the mind is without difference, you are a Buddha complete as you are. There is no need to use mind or effort, still less to contrive or to act; not the least trace of speech or thought is required. Therefore to become a Buddha is the easiest of matters, the most free and unconstrained of matters, and it lies in my own hands, not to be sought outside. If all sentient beings throughout the great earth are unwilling to turn for long kalpas through the four kinds of birth and the six paths, drowned forever in the sea of suffering, and wish instead to become Buddha and dwell in permanence, bliss, self, and purity—then, truly believing the admonitions of the Buddhas and patriarchs, put down everything and think of neither good nor evil, and every one of you may become Buddha on the spot. The Buddhas and bodhisattvas and the patriarchs of every generation vow to save all sentient beings to the last one; this is not without basis, not a vow idly made, not big words idly spoken.
What has been said above is naturally
(by nature)

so, and the Buddhas and patriarchs have again and again elucidated it, earnestly exhorted and instructed, in true and truthful words, without a hair of falsehood. Yet all sentient beings throughout the great earth, from immeasurable kalpas past, have been lost and drowned in the sea of suffering of birth and death, rising and sinking, revolving without cease, deluded and upside down, turning from enlightenment and joining with dust. It is as though pure gold were thrown into a cesspit: not only is it of no use, it becomes defiled beyond bearing. Out of great compassion the Buddha had no choice but to speak the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, so as to
(so as to)

enable sentient beings of every kind and every capacity to counter the eighty-four thousand habitual faults of greed, hatred, delusion, and craving. It is like gold soiled with various stains: one is taught to use a shovel, a brush, water, a cloth, and so on to wash and polish it. Therefore every Dharma the Buddha spoke is a wondrous Dharma, and all can end birth and death and accomplish the Buddha Way; the only question is whether it suits one’s capacity. There is no need to insist on ranking the Dharma gates as high or low. The most widely practiced gates in China are the Chan gate, the teaching schools, the Vinaya, the Pure Land, and the esoteric—these five; according to each person’s faculties and inclinations, any one of them may be practiced. What matters is to go deep into one gate and remain unchanging through the years, and one may then succeed.

The Chan gate chiefly practices investigating Chan, and investigating Chan lies in ‘illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’—that is, penetrating to one’s own original face, what is called ‘clearly awakening to one’s own mind and thoroughly seeing one’s own nature.’ This Dharma gate, from the Buddha’s twirling of a flower down to its transmission to these eastern lands by Patriarch Bodhidharma, has seen its methods of beginning the work change again and again. The Chan worthies before the Tang and Song mostly awakened to the Way from a single word or half a phrase; the transmission between master and disciple was nothing but mind sealing mind, with no real dharma at all. Their daily questions and answers were only the untying of bonds as the occasion required, giving medicine according to the illness.

After the Song dynasty, people’s faculties grew inferior, and they could not do what was taught; for instance, told to ‘put down everything’ and ‘think neither of good nor evil,’ they could never put it down, and were always thinking either of good or of evil. At this juncture the patriarchs had no recourse but to adopt the method of counteracting poison with poison, teaching students to investigate koans. At first it was looking into the huatou, and they even insisted on one dead huatou, telling you to bite down tightly and not relax for an instant, like a mouse gnawing a coffin, biting fast at one place, not stopping until it goes through
if you cannot bite through, you simply die inside it)

; the purpose was to use one thought to oppose ten thousand thoughts. This is truly a method of last resort, like virulent poison in the body: without surgery it is hard to be cured. The koans of the ancients are very many; later they spoke exclusively of looking into the huatou. Some ‘look into who it is that drags this dead corpse about,’ some ‘look into what my original face was before my parents were born’; in recent times the various quarters mostly use the huatou ‘look into who is reciting the Buddha’s name.’ In truth they are all the same, all quite ordinary, nothing strange. If you wanted to look into who it is that recites sutras, who it is that holds mantras, who it is that bows to the Buddha, who it is that eats, who it is that puts on clothes, who it is that walks, who it is that sleeps—it is all one and the same.

[Who is it that drags this dead corpse about] The form-body is dull and insentient, like a dead corpse. ‘Who is it that drags this dead corpse about’ means: who is it that drags this form-body running everywhere? That is to say, who is it that makes the form-body move?

The answer that lies beneath the word ‘who’ is the mind. Speech arises from the mind, and the mind is the head of speech; thoughts arise from the mind, and the mind is the head of thought; all dharmas arise from the mind, and the mind is the head of all dharmas. In truth the huatou is the thought, and what precedes the thought is the mind. Plainly said, the moment before a single thought arises is the huatou. From this you and I know that looking into the huatou is contemplating the mind; the original face before one’s parents were born is the mind, and to look into the original face before one’s parents were born is to contemplate the mind. Nature is mind; ‘turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature’ is turning the contemplation inward to contemplate one’s own mind; ‘perfectly illumining the pure enlightened mark’—the pure enlightened mark is the mind. To illumine is to contemplate, and the mind is Buddha; to recite the Buddha’s name is to contemplate the Buddha, and to contemplate the Buddha is to contemplate the mind. So when we speak of ‘looking into the huatou,’ or of ‘looking into who is reciting the Buddha’s name,’ it is contemplating the mind; it is contemplating and illumining the pure enlightened essence of one’s own mind; it is contemplating the Buddha of one’s own nature. Mind is nature, is enlightenment, is Buddha, without shape or mark, without location, utterly unattainable, pure and naturally so, pervading the Dharma-realm, neither emerging nor entering, neither going nor coming—this is the originally and naturally present pure dharmakāya Buddha.

[Looking into the huatou is contemplating the mind] What is usually called ‘contemplating the mind’ is observing thoughts. The ‘mind’ in this passage refers to self-nature (‘nature is mind’), so ‘contemplating the mind’ here means turning back to observe self-nature. ‘Looking into the huatou is contemplating the mind’ means: looking into the huatou is turning back to observe self-nature.

The practitioner gathers in the six sense-faculties and looks from the place where a single thought first arises, attending to this one huatou, until he sees the pure self-mind apart from thought; then, continuous and dense, calm and bland, he is still and illumines it, and directly the five aggregates are all empty, body and mind both still, not a single thing remaining. From then on, through the six periods of day and night, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, he is thus and unmoving; as days pass and the effort deepens, he sees the nature and becomes Buddha, and all suffering and adversity are crossed over. Formerly Patriarch Gaofeng said: ‘If a student can look into a huatou as though casting a tile into a ten-thousand-fathom pool, straight down to the bottom, and if within seven days he does not awaken, then take this old monk’s head.’ Fellow practitioners, these are the words of one who has been through it, true words and real words, not deceitful words to fool people!

Yet why is it that people today look into the huatou in great numbers, while those who awaken to the Way are few? This is because people today are not the equal of the ancients in faculties, and also because students have mostly not grasped clearly the reasoning of investigating Chan and looking into the huatou. Some go inquiring east and visiting west, running south and rushing north, and in the end, busy until old age, they have not yet made clear just what a huatou
(what it is)

is; they do not know what the huatou is, or how one truly looks into the huatou, and all their lives they cling to words, phrases, names, and marks, applying their minds to the tail of the word. ‘Look into who is reciting the Buddha’s name’—ah! ‘Attend to the huatou’—ah! Looking and looking, investigating and investigating, they run counter to the huatou, east from west; how could they awaken to this naturally so, unconditioned great Way? How could they arrive at the kingly seat that receives nothing at all? Gold dust placed in the eye only blinds it—how could it give forth great radiance! Pitiful, pitiful! Fine sons and daughters leave home to study the Way with no ordinary resolve, and in the end labor in vain—how truly sad and pitiable! The ancients said: ‘Better a thousand years without awakening than a single day on the wrong road.’

In cultivating the Way and awakening to it, what is easy is also hard, and what is hard is also easy. It is like turning on an electric light: if you know how, in the snap of a finger the great light blazes out and the darkness of ten thousand years is suddenly dispelled; if you do not, the machine breaks and the lamp is destroyed, and affliction only increases. Have we not clear examples in those who investigate Chan and look into the huatou and are possessed by demons, go mad, spit blood, contract illness, burn with the fire of ignorance, and deepen their views of self and other? Therefore one who applies effort must also be good at harmonizing body and mind; he must be calm in mind and gentle in temper, with nothing hanging and nothing obstructing, no self and no other, and in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, wondrously accord with the hidden mechanism.

This Dharma of investigating Chan is in itself beyond discrimination, but when it comes to doing the work, the beginner has the beginner’s easiness and difficulty, and the seasoned practitioner has the seasoned practitioner’s. Where lies the beginner’s difficulty? Body and mind are not yet ripe, the road is not clearly found, the effort will not take hold; if he is not fretting inwardly, he is dozing away the days, until at last it becomes ‘the first year a beginner, the second year a veteran, the third year no practice at all.’ And where lies the easiness? One need only be complete in three things: faith, a long-enduring mind, and no-mind.

By faith is meant, first, believing that this mind of mine is originally Buddha, no different from the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times; and second, believing that the Dharma spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha—every single Dharma—can end birth and death and accomplish the Buddha Way.

By the long-enduring mind is meant choosing one Dharma and practicing it to the end of one’s life, and on into the next life and the life after that, always practicing thus: if one investigates Chan, always investigating thus; if one recites the Buddha’s name, always reciting thus; if one holds mantras, always holding thus; if one studies the teachings, always from hearing, reflecting, and practicing. Whatever Dharma gate one practices, one must always take the precepts as the foundation. If one can go on in this way, there is nothing one will not accomplish in the future. Old Master Weishan said: ‘If life after life one does not retreat, the Buddha’s rank may surely be expected.’ And Old Master Yongjia said: ‘If with lying words I deceive sentient beings, may I fall forever into the hell of the pulled-out tongue for dust-mote kalpas.’

By no-mind is meant putting everything down, like a dead man, rising and lying down all day with the community, no longer giving rise to the least discrimination or clinging, and becoming a person of no-mind on the Way.
When a beginner has fulfilled these three minds
(faith, the long-enduring mind, and no-mind)

, and if he investigates Chan and looks into the huatou, he should look into ‘Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?’ Recite ‘Amitābha Buddha’ silently to yourself a few times and see who it is that recites. From where does this one thought arise? You should know that this one thought does not arise from my mouth, nor does it arise from my physical body. If it arose from my body or my mouth, then when I died, though my body and mouth remained, why could they no longer recite? You should know that this one thought arises from my mind,
and from the very place where the thought arises in the mind, fix your gaze upon it at a single peering and look straight on

, like a cat catching a mouse, the whole of one’s spirit concentrated here, with no second thought. But one must moderate the pace, neither too urgent nor too slow, lest illness or obstruction arise. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, it is always thus. As days pass and the effort deepens, when the melon ripens the stem falls, and the time and conditions arrive, touching or bumping against something, one suddenly awakens greatly
(thoroughly seeing one’s own nature)

. At this time it is like a person drinking water, knowing for himself whether it is cold or warm, until he reaches the place of no doubt, like meeting one’s own father at the crossroads, and attains great peace and joy.

What of the easiness and difficulty of the seasoned practitioner? By ‘seasoned practitioner’ is meant one who has drawn near to a good and wise teacher, applied effort for many years, passed through a period of tempering, whose body and mind are ripe and whose course of reasoning is clear, who applies effort at ease and feels no hardship. The difficulty of the seasoned practitioner, the senior of long standing, is that he stops within this ease and clarity, halting at the conjured city and never reaching the jeweled citadel. He can be still but cannot be active, and cannot obtain true benefit; he may even, meeting circumstances, give rise to feeling, taking up and casting off as before, liking and loathing still plain, coarse and subtle delusive thoughts still firm. The effort he applies is like soaking a stone in cold water—it has no effect. In time he slackens, and in the end cannot attain the fruit and bring it into function. If the seasoned practitioner, the senior of long standing, knows this difficulty and at once raises his root huatou, rouses his spirits, and presses on another step from the top of a hundred-foot pole, until he stands on the highest peak and walks in the deepest sea, lets go his hands and ranges at will, and meets the Buddhas and patriarchs face to face—where then is the difficulty? Is it not easy!

The huatou is simply the one mind. This one thought-mind of yours and mine is neither within, between, nor outside, and yet it is within, between, and outside, like space, unmoving yet pervading every place. Therefore the huatou should not be raised upward nor pressed downward: raised up, it gives rise to restlessness; pressed down, it falls into drowsiness; both go against the original mind-nature and are not the Middle Way. Everyone fears delusive thoughts and considers it extremely difficult to subdue them. I tell you all: do not fear delusive thoughts, and do not waste effort trying to subdue them. You need only recognize the delusive thought, not cling to it, not follow after it, not try to drive it away—simply do not continue it, and the delusive thought will depart of itself. This is what is meant by ‘when delusion arises, be aware; awareness is itself freedom from delusion.’ If you can make use of delusive thoughts in your practice, then look into where this delusive thought arises. A delusive thought has no nature of its own; in its very substance it is at once empty, and this restores the mind-nature that is originally mine—the pure self-nature dharmakāya Buddha—and this is right here before you.

To speak truthfully, the real and the illusory are one substance; sentient beings and Buddhas are not two. Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, bodhi and affliction, all are this original mind, this original nature. There is no need to discriminate, no need to delight or loathe, no need to grasp or reject. This mind is pure and is originally Buddha; it needs not so much as a single dharma. How much idle chatter is there in all this—investigate!

blocks.text: The Huatou and the Doubt

inline.s: (Recorded from the “Convenient Teachings of Master Xuyun ·
Chan Hall Instructions

blocks.text: In the Beginning There Was No Huatou

inline.s: The ancient patriarchs pointed directly to the human mind and taught that seeing one’s own nature is becoming Buddha. Thus Patriarch Bodhidharma’s settling of the mind, and the Sixth Patriarch’s sole discussion of seeing the nature—could one but take it up directly and wholeheartedly,
there would have been no need for the huatou

. But by the time of the later patriarchs, seeing that the minds of men were no longer simple and honest, unable to settle down body and soul, and given to much scheming and deception, forever counting the jewels of others as treasures of their own, they had no choice but to establish their own gateways and set forth their own modes of instruction, and only then did they cause students to look into the huatou.

blocks.text: The Head of the Word and the Tail of the Word

inline.s: There are many such topics (huatou): for example, “All things return to the One, but to what does the One return?” and “Before my father and mother were born, what was my original face?” and so on. But “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” is the most common.
What is meant by huatou? “Hua” (the word) is speech, and “tou” (the head) is what precedes speech. For instance, reciting “Amitābha Buddha” is a word;
before the recitation, that is the huatou
. The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises.
The moment a single thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word

. This moment before a thought arises is called “non-arising”: without restlessness, without drowsiness, without clinging to stillness, without falling into emptiness—this is called “non-ceasing.” At all times, solely this one thought turns the light back to reflect. This “non-arising and non-ceasing”
is called looking into the huatou
, or attending to the huatou.

blocks.text: The Doubt Comes First

inline.s: To look into the huatou, one must first arouse the doubt

. The doubt is the staff of looking into the huatou. What is meant by the doubt? For example, when one asks who it is that recites the Buddha’s name, everyone knows that it is oneself who recites. But is it recited with the mouth, or is it recited with the mind? If it is recited with the mouth, then when one is asleep the mouth is still present—why then does it not recite? If it is recited with the mind, what does the mind look like? There is nowhere to grasp it, and so one does not understand. Thus, upon the word “who,” one raises a subtle, slight
thought of doubt
, but it should not be coarse; the finer the better. At all times and in all places,
solely attending to and steadying this thought of doubt

, gazing at it continuously like flowing water, without giving rise to a second thought. If the thought of doubt is present, do not stir it; if the thought of doubt is absent, raise it up gently again. When one first applies the mind, one will surely find more strength in stillness than in activity. But one must never give rise to a discriminating mind—do not concern yourself with whether it is effective or not, do not concern yourself with whether it is in activity or in stillness. Just apply your effort with one whole mind
[To look into the huatou, one must first arouse the doubt]
Then how does one arouse the doubt? Elder Master Xuyun said: “Begin by investigating the tail of the word.” In his “Two Letters to Layman Jin Hongshu (

),” Elder Master Xuyun said: “If a beginner applies effort, he cannot but investigate from the tail of the word. For the sentient beings of the Latter Age of the Dharma are thick in obstructions and shallow in wisdom; without beginning from the tail of the word, it is hard to reach the huatou; without applying effort at the place where the conscious mind is, it is hard to realize the mind that is without thought.” In the “Admonitions on Chan Practice,” Elder Master Xuyun said: “If you have not yet seen the huatou (the head, that which precedes the word), and your idle thoughts and drowsiness are many, then you should still look at the word ‘who’ in ‘Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?’ When you have seen it so that idle thoughts and drowsiness are few, and the word ‘who’ can no longer be forgotten, then look at the very place where this single thought arises. When a single thought no longer arises, that is non-arising; to be able to see the non-arising of a single thought is called truly looking into the huatou.”

blocks.text: First Investigate the Tail of the Word

inline.s: Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?”—the four characters place the greatest weight on the single word “who.” The other three characters merely indicate the general matter. For instance, who is it that puts on clothes and eats? Who is it that defecates and urinates? Who is it that gives rise to ignorance? Who is it that knows and is aware? Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, once the word “who” is raised it most easily gives rise to a thought of doubt, without waiting for repeated pondering, conjecture, or deliberate intention. For this reason, the “who” word as huatou is truly a wondrous method of Chan practice.

But this is not taking the word “who” or the four characters “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” and reciting them as a Buddha-name, nor is it the pondering and conjecture of seeking out who it is that recites the Buddha’s name and calling that the doubt. There be some
(certain people)

who recite the four characters “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” without ever stopping; this is not as meritorious as reciting a single “Amitābha Buddha.” There be others who let their thoughts run wild and search here and there, and call that the doubt—little do they know that the more they think, the more idle thoughts arise, which is like wishing to rise yet falling instead. One must know this.

blocks.text: The Doubt Manifests

inline.s: The doubting thought of a beginner is very coarse, now broken off and now resumed, now familiar and now new. It does not count as the doubt; it may only be called thinking. Gradually, as the wild mind is reined in and the thought can be held a little steady,
then it is called investigating (can)

. Further, as the effort gradually ripens, one later doubts without intending to doubt. One no longer is aware of where one sits, nor does one know of body, mind, or world. Solely the thought of doubt appears before one, unbroken and uninterrupted, and then
this is called the doubt
. In truth, to speak practically—does that earlier stage count as real effort? It is merely beating up idle fancies.
Only when the true doubt
(the genuine doubt—thought after thought, without interruption, investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
now appears
—that is the time of true effort.

blocks.text: Raising Awareness and Illumination

inline.s: This is a great pass, where one can very easily run off onto a wrong path

[Guān’ài (a strategic pass)]A strategically vital defile. [This is a great pass]This is a great and dangerous pass. When one’s effort reaches the stage of “doubting without intending to doubt, no longer aware of where one sits, no longer knowing body, mind, or world, solely the thought of doubt appearing before one, unbroken and uninterrupted,” then the following pure and clear states appear. If one cannot handle them properly, one can very easily run off onto a wrong path.

1. At this time one is pure and clear, with boundless ease and well-being. Should one lose awareness and illumination even slightly, one sinks into a state of light drowsiness. Were there a person with clear eyes at one’s side, he would see at a glance that one is dwelling in this realm, and with a single blow of the incense board the clouds and mists would instantly disperse—and many have thereby awakened to the Way.

2. At this time one is pure and clear, empty and hollow. If the doubt has vanished, this is the indifferent state, sitting on a withered-tree crag, or what is called “soaking rocks in cold water.” At this point one must raise it—
to raise is awareness and illumination

. Awareness means not being deluded, and that is wisdom; illumination means not being disturbed, and that is samādhi. Solely this single thought, clear and still, as calm and unmoving, numinously undimmed, constantly aware—like cold fire drawing forth smoke, a single thread stretching on without breaking.
[Solely this single thought]Merely this one thought of awareness and illumination, and nothing else.

blocks.text: Do Not Raise It Again

inline.s: When effort has reached this stage, one must possess the diamond (vajra) eye—
no longer raise it

, for raising is placing a head upon a head. Formerly a monk asked the Old Master Zhaozhou: “When not a single thing is brought, what then?” Zhaozhou said: “Put it down.” The monk said: “If not a single thing is brought, what is there to put down?” Zhaozhou said: “If you cannot put it down, take it up and carry it.” This is precisely speaking of this juncture. The scenery within it is like a person drinking water, who knows for himself whether it is warm or cold; it cannot be reached by words. One who has reached this stage naturally understands; one who has not reached this stage gains nothing from being told. As the saying goes, “Meeting a swordsman by the way, one must present a sword; it is not for a poet to offer a poem.”
[When effort has reached this stage]the application of effort reaching

the stage of “solely this single thought, clear and still, as calm and unmoving, numinously undimmed, constantly aware—like cold fire drawing forth smoke, a single thread stretching on without breaking.” [No longer raise it]At this point, although one no longer raises awareness and illumination, the illumination is still present, illumining of itself—this is called silent illumination. Still, it is ever illumining; illumining, it is ever still. Master Dayu’s verse says: “Silent illumination, illumining stillness—above all, do not use force. To become a Buddha and be master, there is no other secret.” This is precisely what is meant by this realm of silent illumination.

blocks.text: The Instructions of the Venerable Grand Master

inline.s: Recorded from
Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions
In the thirty-sixth year of the Republic
, during the winter Chan session, I went up to the abbot’s quarters to request instructions.
The Grand Master asked me: “What practice do you use?”
I said: “I also recite the Buddha’s name and also investigate Chan, practicing Chan and Pure Land in tandem.”
He asked: “Since you recite the Buddha’s name, how can you also investigate Chan?”
I said: “When I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind holds the doubt of who it is that is reciting the Buddha’s name; so although I am reciting the Buddha’s name, it is at the same time Chan practice.”

He asked: “Are there idle thoughts?” I answered: “When right mindfulness is raised, delusive thoughts often arise following along behind it. When right mindfulness is set down, then there are no delusive thoughts either—pure and free.”

The Grand Master said: “This purity and freedom are laziness and sloth—soaking rocks in cold water; even cultivating for a thousand years would be a waste. You must surely raise right mindfulness and investigate with fierce vigor, and see through to who it is who is ultimately reciting the Buddha’s name. Only then can you break through. You must apply effort with diligence.”
He asked: “I have heard that, at Zhongnan Mountain, the Grand Master entered samādhi for eighteen days. Did he enter with a mind, or without a mind?”

I answered: “Entering samādhi with a mind, one surely cannot be settled. Entering samādhi without a mind is like a statue of clay or wood. When the mind is held to a single place, nothing is left undone.”
He asked: “I wish to learn from the Grand Master how to enter samādhi; please teach me, Grand Master.”
I answered: “It is impossible without looking into the huatou.”
He asked: “What is called the huatou?”
He answered: “‘Hua’ (the word) is idle thought—one’s own talking to oneself.
In the place where idle thoughts have not yet arisen, observe and watch: see what the original face is. This is called looking into the huatou.

When idle thoughts have already arisen, still raise right mindfulness, and the wrong thought will vanish of itself. If one follows after idle thoughts, sitting in meditation is of no benefit. If one raises right mindfulness but it is not earnest, then the huatou is without strength and the delusive thoughts must arise. Therefore, in applying effort one must be fierce and diligent, as if mourning one’s own parents. An ancient worthy said: ‘Learning the Way is like guarding a walled city; tightly guard the city wall through a whole battle. Without once enduring the cold that pierces the very bone, how could the plum blossom greet the nose with its fragrance?’ (These words the Grand Master would repeat at every session.)
If there are no idle thoughts, then neither is there a huatou. Sitting still with an empty mind, soaking rocks in cold water—even sitting through countless eons brings no benefit.

If one does not investigate Chan, so be it; but once one has resolved to investigate, one must be fierce and diligent, like a single man contending against ten thousand, advancing straight ahead without retreating, not relaxing in the least. Reciting the Buddha’s name is likewise; holding the mantra is likewise. When the thought of birth-and-death is earnest, and each day becomes more pressing than the last, then the effort will make progress.”

blocks.text: Attending to the Huatou and Turning the Hearing Inward to Self-Nature

inline.s: Excerpted from Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions · Chan Hall Instructions.

What is meant by huatou? “Hua” (the word) is speech, and “tou” (the head) is what precedes speech. For instance, reciting “Amitābha Buddha” is a word; before the recitation, that is the huatou. The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises; the moment a single thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word. This moment before a thought arises is called “non-arising”; without restlessness, without drowsiness, without clinging to stillness, without falling into emptiness, it is called “non-ceasing.” At all times, solely this single thought turns the light back to reflect upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing”—this is called looking into the huatou, or attending to the huatou.

[Non-arising and non-ceasing]The “non-arising and non-ceasing” spoken of here means: a single thought does not arise, and the investigation does not cease (without restlessness, without drowsiness, without clinging to stillness, without falling into emptiness). [Restlessness (diāojǔ)]The agitation of mental thought.
Someone asks
(a person asks)
: “How is it evident that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara’s turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature is Chan practice?”

[Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature is precisely Chan practice]When Elder Master Xuyun spoke in the “Chan Hall Instructions” about the method of Chan practice, he said: “Though the methods of practice are many, all the Buddhas and patriarchs regard Chan practice as the supreme, wondrous gateway. At the Śūraṅgama assembly, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva to select the path of perfect penetration, and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s perfect penetration of the ear faculty was deemed the foremost. When we turn the hearing inward to hear self-nature, that is Chan practice.”
I just
(just now)
said that attending to the huatou means teaching you, at all times, solely this single thought, turning the light back to reflect upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing.”
Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature also means teaching you, at all times, solely this single thought, turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature.

“Turning” means going against; “non-arising and non-ceasing” is self-nature. Although, when flowing downstream, “hearing” and “illuminating” follow sounds and chase after forms—the hearing not going beyond the sound, the seeing not going beyond the form, with discrimination plainly apparent—yet when one goes against the stream and reversely observes self-nature, not following sounds nor chasing after forms, then it is originally a single pure awareness, and “hearing” and “illuminating” are not two different things. We must know: the so-called attending to the huatou, the so-called turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature, is absolutely not looking with the eyes, nor listening with the ears. Were one to look with the eyes or listen with the ears, that would be following sounds and chasing after forms, being turned by objects, which is called flowing downstream. If solely this single thought dwells in “non-arising and non-ceasing,” not following sounds nor chasing after forms, that is called going against the stream, called attending to the huatou, and also called turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature.

[Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature]The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature, the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.” Regarding turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature, there is a most brilliant passage in the “Essentials of Cultivating the Mind”: “There are many ways of entering the principle; I point out to you a single gate, to bring you back to the source. Do you still hear the cawing of crows and the chatter of magpies?” “I do.” “Then turn your hearing back upon your own hearing-nature. Are there still many sounds?” “When I arrive here, all sounds and all discriminations are entirely unobtainable.” “How wonderful! How wonderful! This is Avalokiteśvara’s gate of entering the principle. I ask you further: you say that when you arrive here, all sounds and all discriminations are entirely unobtainable. Since they are unobtainable, at that very moment—is it not emptiness?” “Originally it is not empty; it is clearly luminous, not dimmed.” “What then is the substance of the non-empty?” “It has no appearance either; it cannot be reached by words.” “This is the life-span of all the Buddhas and all the patriarchs; doubt it no more.” [One pure awareness (yījīngmíng)]Refers to the pure mind of self-nature originally possessed by every person. “Pure and subtle” describes its bright, clear, and wondrous quality. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “Originally based upon a single pure awareness, it is divided into a sixfold union.” A single pure awareness is the one mind. The sixfold union is the union of the six faculties with the six objects: the eye with form, the ear with sound, the nose with fragrance, the tongue with taste, the body with touch, and the mind with dharmas.

blocks.text: A Letter on Chan

inline.s: Excerpted from Old Master Xuyun’s Letter on Chan.
I often lament that the Dharma door
(the Chan gate)
has fallen into decay, and that genuine teachers
(good and wise teachers)
are rarely heard of. Yet those who study are as plentiful as the hairs of an ox,
(a metaphor for very many)
while those who accomplish are like the horns of a rabbit
(a metaphor for not a single one)
—all because they themselves lack the eye and ear,
(that is, because their course of reasoning is not clear)

and have erred in their proper tuning. Therefore the ancient worthy said: to have people look into the huatou, one must put down the whole body, as if one were a corpse, solely raise this single thought and carry it into investigation, and arouse the doubt.
Doubt what? Since it is called the head of the word, it has long since fallen to the tail of the word. One must know that the true huatou
is to be investigated toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted
. Without distinguishing activity from stillness, thought after thought without interval,
this is called the doubt

(To investigate—without distinguishing activity from stillness, thought after thought without interval—toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted is called the doubt. Note: here “the doubt” is the doubt of looking into the huatou, whereas the “doubt” spoken of in the earlier section “The Huatou and the Doubt” is the doubt of investigating the tail of the word.)
Doubt on and doubt on, until it is beaten into a single mass.
(After the doubt is beaten into a single mass,)
turn the light back and shine upon it: who is it that doubts? After a long, long time, when the melon ripens the stem falls; suddenly one touches the nostrils with which one was born
(thoroughly seeing one’s own nature)
, not obtained from outside.

[Since it is called the head of the word, it has long since fallen to the tail of the word]To suppose that a sentence or a single character is the huatou is in fact already the tail of the word. In Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions · Chan Hall Instructions, Elder Master Xuyun said: “The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises; the moment a single thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word.” [The three stages of Chan practice]First,

investigate toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted, until the doubt is beaten into a single mass; second, turn the light back and shine upon it, asking who it is that doubts; third, (after a long, long time,) when the melon ripens the stem falls, thoroughly seeing one’s own nature.
Therefore the Eternal Patriarch
(Master Yongjia)

said: “In walking there is Chan, in sitting there is Chan; whether speaking or silent, in movement or in stillness, the essence is at ease.” Practicing thus, what difficulty is there? From where does the sickness arise? The so-called “wild mind” is nothing but the mixed poisons of the past. One does not know that beneath the Chan school even a single word is of no use, and that Buddha and demon are cut off alike.

[Mixed poisons]All views, mysterious sayings, and wondrous words. Master Hanshan said: “The method of using the mind is to single-mindedly raise the thought of the upward task; you must strike at the very place where the Buddhas and patriarchs have no place, and plant your heels firmly. Next, you must spit out all at once the views, mysterious sayings, and wondrous words in your breast, which are mixed poisons.” (Dream Roaming Collection · Instructions to the Chan Practitioner Shuanglunzhao). He also said: “This matter (seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha) is originally possessed by every person, without any deficiency, complete and full. That it is not known in daily use and not received in benefit is precisely because the evil seeds of beginningless habitual tendencies have been accumulated over eons and deeply entrenched, so that they have long been hard to uproot. Now, newly refined with the words of teaching and letters, the gong’an (public cases) of the patriarchs, and views of every kind, an additional layer of obstruction is added. Though one seeks to be clear about oneself, the more one seeks the further one is. Why is this so? Only because, being blind to oneself, one seeks and takes from outside. Because the afflictions and habitual tendencies accumulated over many lives are called the affliction-obstruction, while mysterious views are called the knowledge-obstruction. If these two obstructions are eliminated, the essence itself is revealed. Now, in investigating the upward matter, first let go of the entire literary language, mysterious principles, and learning of the past, and name them mixed poisons, spitting them out utterly. Solely raise your own original huatou, lay down the doubt anew, and cut off the very root of idle thoughts and afflictions, so that within cannot come out and without cannot enter. When the boundary of before and after is cut, the middle is isolated of itself, and there is only a single ball of doubt as the very life-root of your own being. Doubt on until you can doubt no further, and at the place where no strength can be applied, gaze fixedly and see what after all it is. Looking and looking, pressing and pressing, there will of itself come a time when the matter collapses. But leave so much as a hair’s breadth of views in it, and you are separated by a thousand, ten thousand miles. Just look at the First Patriarch (Patriarch Bodhidharma), who said: ‘Making the mind like a wall, one may enter the Way’—this is the first road of returning home. If the mind is unwilling to die and the doubt is not to the point, then for a thousand lives and a hundred eons one will remain forever on the road. Abbot, just gather your spirit into this, and I assure you that, on the day of attainment, it will surely not be a place that the empty bookish phrases of “zhi, hu, zhe, ye” can reach. Strive with all your might!” (Dream Roaming Collection · Instructions to the Lay Abbot Zhixian) [Collapse (dàoduàn)]The conclusion. Here it means thoroughly seeing one’s own nature.

As for what is called activity and stillness, the beginner in study cannot but investigate it. Walking, standing, being in the hall, at work, receiving and seeing off guests, talking and laughing, urinating and defecating—these are called activity; sitting and lying down in quietness are called stillness. Examine it subtly in this way
(examine it subtly in this way)
: in the course of the six periods of the day and night
(in the course of my present twenty-four hours)
, at what time am I in activity without being carried off by activity
(still investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? At what time am I in stillness without being turned by stillness
(still investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? In the presence of all circumstances, does the mind arise or not arise? If one can examine as before
(if one truly can examine in this way)
, then in activity, not being carried off by activity
(not giving rise to delusive thoughts in activity)
, one can be alert and still
(alert and at the same time still)
; in stillness, not being turned by stillness
(in stillness, not sinking into drowsiness)
, one is still and alert
(quiet and at the same time alert)

This is merely the awakening of your beginner’s mind. In activity and stillness do not lean and wither to one side; be certain that activity and stillness are one suchness, with matter and principle wholly interfused. This is just what the Twenty-seventh Patriarch
(the Twenty-seventh Patriarch of the Western Heaven, the Venerable Prajñātāra, the teacher of Patriarch Bodhidharma)

said: “In the in-breath I do not dwell in the realms of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch the many conditions; thus I ever turn such a sūtra—a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls.”

[The realms of the aggregates (yīnjie)]The five aggregates and the eighteen realms. [Five aggregates (wǔyīn)]An older translation of the five skandhas; “yīn” carries the sense of veiling—it can veil the true reality of thusness and give rise to all afflictions. [Five skandhas]Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the five great elements constituting the human person. The aggregate of form is the body; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the mind. [Eighteen realms]The union of the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the six objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas; and the six consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these together are called the “eighteen realms.”

[In the in-breath I do not dwell in the realms of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch the many conditions]This is an instance of “mutual wording,” meaning: the in-breath (inhaling) and the out-breath (exhaling) are not deluded by body and mind, and the in-breath and the out-breath are not deluded by realms and conditions. In other words, at no time is one deluded by body and mind or by realms and conditions. [Mutual wording (hùwén)]Mutual wording, also called “mutual phrasing,” is a rhetorical device commonly used in Classical Chinese. Its characteristic is that it is neither verbose nor redundant nor flat and straightforward, but subtle and condensed, with the wording spare while the meaning is preserved; the two parts complement each other to reveal the sense and reflect off each other with radiance. For example, in the “Ballad of Mulan,” “generals die in a hundred battles, warriors return after ten years” means: generals and warriors die in a hundred battles, and generals and warriors return after ten years. Another example is in the “Record of the Yueyang Tower,” “not rejoicing over things, not grieving over oneself,” which means: not rejoicing because of things or self, and likewise not grieving because of things or self. Here “things” refers to people other than oneself and the circumstances in which one lives, while “self” refers to one’s personal lot.

[In the in-breath I do not dwell in the realms of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch the many conditions; thus I ever turn such a sūtra—a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls]The in-breath and the out-breath are not deluded by body and mind, are not deluded by realms and conditions; to ever recite such a sūtra (taking ultimate reality as the sūtra) is equivalent to reciting a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls of sūtras. The “Congrong Record” says: “The king of Eastern India invited the Twenty-seventh Patriarch Prajñātāra. During the meal, the king asked: ‘Why do you not read the sūtras?’ The Patriarch said: ‘This poor monk’s in-breath does not dwell in the realms of the aggregates, and the out-breath does not touch the many conditions; thus I ever turn such a sūtra—a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls.’” [Turning the sūtra]Reciting the sūtra. The “Biographies of Eminent Monks · On Sūtra Readers” says: “Chanting sūtras is called turning and reading; singing praise is called Sanskrit voice.” [During the meal (zhāicì)]At the table during the vegetarian feast. “Cì” carries the sense of “in the midst of,” as in “in the breast” (xiōngcì) and “at the table” (xícì).
Beyond thought and discussion
(one must not go about thinking and discussing; in Chan practice one must not use the mind of consciousness to ponder, conjecture, or argue)

. Never seek after words, turn with the tongue-roots of others, and exhaust one’s very spirit to no real benefit. Sitting on the rush cushion, one dozes and is dull; when one unbends the legs, one idly chatters. When one meets circumstances and sounds
(conditions)
, one has no mastery whatsoever. How bitter! Let each of you be careful.
Note: The “Old Master Xuyun’s Letter on Chan” was originally published in “Sound of the Sea Tide” (Haichao Yin), Year Ten, Issue Four, and should be
, a letter that Elder Master Xuyun wrote around that time to his disciple Master Xiuyuan, giving instructions on investigating the huatou.

blocks.text: The Two Kinds of Easiness and Difficulty in Practice

inline.s: For those who apply effort in the cultivation of the Way, in terms of the depth or shallowness of their practice, there are two kinds of easiness and difficulty: first, the easiness and difficulty of the beginner’s effort; second, the easiness and difficulty of the seasoned practitioner’s effort.

blocks.text: 1. The Easiness and Difficulty of the Beginner’s Effort

inline.s: [The thieving mind (tōuxīn)]The mind that grasps at conditions. Because this mind of grasping at conditions steals the Dharma-wealth, keeping the true Dharma from appearing, the Chan grove calls it the thieving mind. The “Anheidou Collection” says:
“While the thieving mind is not dead, it is the great affliction of the student.”

[The mind that grasps at conditions (pānyuánxīn)]The mind that arises by grasping at the six objects; it is also called the deliberating mind. [Dharma-wealth (fǎcái)]The counterpart of “worldly wealth,” referring to the Buddha-Dharma. Because the Buddha-Dharma can moisten and nourish sentient beings and is the provision for nurturing their wisdom-life, just as worldly treasure is, it is metaphorically called Dharma-wealth.

The common sickness of the beginner’s effort is that the habitual tendencies of idle thinking cannot be put down—ignorance and conceit, jealousy and obstruction, greed, hatred, delusion, and craving, idleness and a taste for fine food, right and wrong and self-and-others fill up a whole belly. How could such a one be in accord with the Way?
[Conceit (gònggāo)]Arrogance and self-importance.

Or there be one who comes of a family of pampered young gentlemen, whose old habits are not forgotten, who cannot endure the least grievance, who cannot bear the slightest hardship—how could such a one apply effort in the Way? He never considers what sort of person the original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha was when he left the home life.
Or there be some who have learned a few characters, yet do not understand that the questions in the recorded sayings of the ancient worthies are meant to test the depth or shallowness of the student
(to test the depth or shallowness of the student’s practice)

; so they fancy themselves clever, and all day long hunt for phrases and sentences, discoursing on mind and on Buddha, taking the words of the ancients as something to be understood and explained. Doing this business of talking about food and counting treasures, they still think themselves remarkable and give rise to great arrogance. When they meet a serious illness, they cry out in bitter distress; or when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives
(or when death arrives)
, they are flustered and confused. The knowledge and understanding of their whole life is of no use at all—only then do they regret it too late.

There is yet another kind of person who twists the saying “Originally a Buddha, not belonging to cultivation and realization.” He says that it is originally complete and need not be cultivated or realized, and all day long he is listless and scattered, indulging his feelings and giving free rein. Wasting his time, he still calls himself “an extraordinary man, free and at ease amid conditions.” Such a person is going to suffer bitter consequences.
One who has some mind of the Way, again, cannot find a place to start.

Or there be one who is afraid of idle thoughts, and can neither get rid of them; all day long vexed and troubled, blaming himself for his heavy karmic obstructions, he thereby loses the mind of the Way.

Or there be one who wants to fight to the death with idle thoughts, angrily clenching his fists and puffing up his breath, sticking out his chest and staring wide-eyed, as if in earnest, about to wage a war to the death with idle thoughts; little does he know that idle thoughts cannot be fought to the death, and that instead he will end up spewing blood and going mad.
Or there be one who fears falling into emptiness; little does he know that a “ghost” has already been born, that the emptiness cannot be emptied away and enlightenment cannot be attained.
Or there be one who uses the mind to seek enlightenment; little does he know that seeking to enlighten and wishing to become a Buddha are all a great idle thought. Sand is not the basis of rice
(boiling sand cannot make rice)
; seek until the “year of the donkey,” and one will certainly never attain enlightenment.

Or there be one who, hitting upon a stick or two of quiet incense, gives rise to a feeling of joy. That is merely the blind-eyed turtle praising a hole in a log—happening upon it by chance, not genuine practice; and it is an extra layer of the obstruction of joy.
[A stick or two of quiet incense]During that stick or two of incense, the mind is pure, clear, and still.
Or there be one who in stillness feels pure, clear, and comfortable, but in activity cannot manage; so he flees noise for stillness and sits in dead water, passing his days.
Such cases are many, very many.
For the beginner who cannot find the path, it is truly difficult: with awareness but without illumination, one is scattered and cannot “settle into the hall”
(for the mind is scattered and the effort cannot come to rest in the hall)
; with illumination but without awareness, one again sits soaked and drowned in dead water.

Though applying effort is said to be difficult, once one finds the path it is quite easy. What is the easiness of the beginner’s effort? There is no cleverness to it—just let go. Let go of what? Just let go of all ignorance and affliction.

Fellow practitioners all! This body of ours, when one breath does not come, is a corpse. The reason we cannot let go is only that we value it heavily; hence self and other, right and wrong, love and hate, grasping and rejecting arise. If one were certain that this body is a corpse, not treasuring it, and not regarding it as “I” in the least, what would there be to let go of?

Provided one can let go, then at all times and in all places, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, in activity or stillness, busy or free, the whole body within and without is cold and still, only a single thought of doubt, peacefully and continuously doubting on, without the slightest admixture of another thought. A single huatou is like a great sword leaning against the sky; whoever touches its blade has his traces wiped out and his voice silenced. What idle thoughts are there to fear? What idle fellow can strike you? Who goes to distinguish activity from stillness? Who has recourse to existence or emptiness?

If one fears idle thoughts, that adds one more layer of idle thought; if one is aware of being pure and clear, it has long since ceased to be pure and clear; if one fears falling into emptiness, one has already sunk into existence; if one wishes to become a Buddha, one has already entered the demonic path.
Therefore, so long as one recognizes the path
(the path is this single thought of letting everything go and single-mindedly raising the huatou)

, then carrying water and hauling firewood are none other than the wondrous Way, and hoeing the fields and planting the soil are always the living meaning of Chan. It is not only by sitting cross-legged in meditation all day that one is counted as applying effort in the cultivation of the Way.

blocks.text: 2. The Easiness and Difficulty of the Seasoned Practitioner’s Effort

inline.s: What, then, is the difficulty of the seasoned practitioner’s effort? When his effort carries him to the point where true doubt stands before him—to have awareness and illumination still belongs to birth-and-death; to have neither awareness nor illumination falls again into vacant nothingness. This ground is truly hard, and many who reach it cannot shake themselves free; they stand atop the hundred-foot pole with no way to advance.

[True doubt]The genuine doubt-sensation—probing, thought after thought without interruption, toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted. [Standing atop the hundred-foot pole, unable to advance]Daoyuan
the Chan Master’s verse reads
“A man unmoving atop the hundred-foot pole
not a single thought arising
, though he has entered, is not yet true
not ultimate
; from the hundred-foot pole he must step forward
seeing the nature through and through
, and the ten directions of the world are the whole body.”
(Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
There are some
(certain people)

who, having reached this ground, find their effort a little under control and meet no situation they cannot break through, and so imagine that ignorance is utterly cut off and their effort has arrived home. Little do they know that they are living every day inside the cave of ignorance without knowing it. Suddenly meeting a single situation, they cannot break through it, cannot be their own master, and are carried off by it as before—how regrettable!

Or there are those who reach the ground where true doubt stands before them, and in that emptiness a little wisdom arises; having savoured a few koans of the ancients, they let go of the doubt-sensation, fancy themselves greatly awakened, chant poems and compose verses, blink their eyes and lift their brows, and call themselves good and wise teachers. Such people ruin themselves and ruin others; their offence is boundless.

There are also those who mistake the meaning of Old Man Bodhidharma’s “Outwardly, cease all conditions; inwardly, let the mind be without gasping; with a mind like a wall, one may enter the Way,” and of the Sixth Patriarch’s “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at precisely this
nèn

moment—what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?”—and so they take sitting beside a withered tree on a rocky ledge as the ultimate standard. Such people take the conjured city for the treasure city and a guest land for their native home; the old woman burning down the hut is precisely a curse upon these dead fellows.

[Misunderstanding the meaning]1.
